title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
trick: Plant two conflicting numbers in document-review tasks and count per stage whether both survive worker reads, worker summaries and the lead's report: forced delegation reads more pairs, summaries drop most, fewer conflicts get flagged.
framing_stripped: Called 'multi-agent memory inconsistency' studied with a 'benchmark and evidence-flow profiler' and 'Pair Recall' (sec. 3); it is a string matcher ('fact-specific anchors and verified equivalent representations', sec. 3.3) that checks whether two planted numbers both appear in the captured text of four stages (tool outputs, outgoing worker messages, the lead's inbox plus its own reads, the graded report) for 73 conflicts x 3 models x 3 delegation policies x 2 runs under one $59.60 per-task allowance, with an LLM judge (claude-sonnet-5) deciding whether the report flagged the conflict; the headline is pooled over 438 observations per policy: forced delegation retrieves both numbers in 68.7% vs 50.2% for a single agent but the judge passes 13.2% vs 16.2% (Table 1), the pair count falls from 301 to 107 between worker reads and worker reports (sec. 4.3), and on matched cases forced delegation beats the single agent when one worker read both numbers (34.2% vs 22.5% of 111) and loses when the numbers were split across workers (10.0% vs 18.9% of 190; sec. 4.4).
method_equations: Benchmark (sec. 3.1): 11 Harvey LAB due-diligence tasks (Grupen et al., 2026; agents review document directories and write red-flags reports). To plant conflict $i$, 'we replace selected appearances of a recurring numerical value' $A_i$ with $B_i$ in designated directories, leaving $A_i$ unchanged elsewhere; 'Five to seven conflicts appear per task, totaling 73; all conflicts in a task are evaluated against the same report.' 'The evaluator keeps the conflict specifications and grading rubrics separate from the agent inputs.' Policies (sec. 3.2): None, 'one agent inspects documents and writes the report'; Optional, 'the lead may inspect sources itself, create workers, and assign overlapping reviews'; Required, 'workers inspect assigned document partitions while the lead coordinates and synthesizes their findings without reading source documents'; 'Workers can also contribute to a shared report draft'; 'Optional and Required permit up to ten concurrent workers, with additional instances possible across continuation phases.' Profiler (sec. 3.3): 'captures model requests and responses through a local proxy and correlates them with SDK events, native traces, tool outputs, and report artifacts'; 'Agent and tool-call identifiers attribute evidence to its reader, sender, or recipient within the trajectory prefix that produced the graded report'; 'Source evidence is counted from returned content, including search excerpts.' Four stages: Source Reads 'captures endpoints visible in source-tool outputs'; Worker Reports 'captures outgoing worker messages and completion reports, including peer-directed messages'; Lead Evidence 'combines incoming evidence with the lead’s permitted source reads'; Final Report 'contains endpoints in the selected, graded deliverable'. 'Source Reads, Worker Reports, and Lead Evidence accumulate observations through the graded checkpoint; Final Report measures the selected deliverable.' 'We track outgoing messages and incoming receipts separately, using plaintext collaboration traces for GPT-6 delegated executions.' Metric (sec. 3.4, eq. 1): for conflict observation $i$ with planted pair $G_i = \{A_i, B_i\}$ and $E_i^t$ the set of endpoints observed at stage $t$, pooled across eligible agents or artifacts, $$R^{t}_{\mathrm{pair}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{1}\left[G_i \subseteq E_i^t\right],$$ where $N$ is the number of conflict observations and $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ equals 1 when both endpoints are present ('A conflict earns pair credit when both endpoints are present, regardless of unrelated evidence'). At the first three stages $R^{t}_{\mathrm{pair}} = R^{t}_{\mathrm{same}} + R^{t}_{\mathrm{split}}$: Same when one individual supplies both endpoints, Split when only the contributors' union contains both, 'Same takes precedence when multiple routes exist'; 'These labels describe cumulative provenance across the trajectory, identifying readers at Source Reads, sending workers at Worker Reports, and immediate contributors at Lead Evidence.' Final Report uses Both with no Same/Split split. Judge Pass (sec. 3.4): an LLM judge (claude-sonnet-5); 'Our rubric has two criteria per conflict: identifying the discrepancy and accurately treating its quantitative comparison'; Judge Pass 'requires both criteria, including an explicit flag for the specified conflict; its rate measures conflict detection.' Setup (sec. 4.1): GPT-5.6 Luna and GPT-6 Luna through the Codex SDK, Claude Haiku 5.5 through the Claude Code SDK; 'Each model runs each policy twice on all 11 tasks, yielding 198 task executions and 1,314 conflict observations', $n = 146$ per model/policy and $n = 438$ per pooled policy, 'with repeated conflicts clustered within tasks'. 'Generation uses common per-task dollar allowances totaling $59.60 per round.' 'When spending remains below a configured fraction of the allowance, the system continues its native session to review and revise the report, retaining its history and cumulative spending.' 'Accounting covers all lead and worker calls, including revisions, compaction, and paid interruptions; judging is excluded.' Mean spending 0.95 to 1.02 times the allowance. Table 1 (percent of 146 per model/policy, 438 pooled; columns: Source Reads Total/Same/Split; Worker Reports Total/Same/Split; Lead Evidence Total/Same/Split; Final Report Both; Judge Pass; Cost as a fraction of the $59.60 allowance). GPT-5.6 Luna: None 69.9/69.9/0.0; no worker channel; 69.9/69.9/0.0; 21.2; 15.8; 0.96. Optional 67.1/65.1/2.1; 0.7/0.7/0.0; 63.0/63.0/0.0; 26.0; 23.3; 0.95. Required 78.8/32.9/45.9; 24.0/18.5/5.5; 24.0/18.5/5.5; 11.6; 10.3; 1.02. GPT-6 Luna: None 59.6/59.6/0.0; no worker channel; 59.6/59.6/0.0; 17.8; 17.1; 0.95. Optional 65.1/63.7/1.4; 0.7/0.7/0.0; 63.7/63.7/0.0; 19.9; 19.2; 0.95. Required 61.6/26.0/35.6; 18.5/13.0/5.5; 18.5/13.0/5.5; 12.3; 11.6; 0.96. Claude Haiku 5.5: None 21.2/21.2/0.0; no worker channel; 21.2/21.2/0.0; 15.8; 15.8; 0.95. Optional 56.2/24.0/32.2; 37.0/24.7/12.3; 37.7/28.8/8.9; 31.5; 30.1; 0.98. Required 65.8/17.1/48.6; 30.8/17.8/13.0; 30.8/17.8/13.0; 23.3; 17.8; 0.97. Pooled: None 50.2/50.2/0.0; no worker channel; 50.2/50.2/0.0; 18.3; 16.2; 0.95. Optional 62.8/50.9/11.9; 12.8/8.7/4.1; 54.8/51.8/3.0; 25.8; 24.2; 0.96. Required 68.7/25.3/43.4; 24.4/16.4/8.0; 24.4/16.4/8.0; 15.8; 13.2; 0.98. Per model (sec. 4.3): 'Relative to None, Required raises Source Reads Pair Recall by 8.9 percentage points (pp) for GPT-5.6 and 2.1 pp for GPT-6, while detection falls by 5.5 pp for each. Haiku gains 44.5 pp in Source Pair Recall but only 2.1 pp in detection. Optional has the highest detection rate for all three models.' Counts (sec. 4.3): 'Across all 438 Required observations, Source Reads contain both claims in 301 cases (68.7%), compared with 107 (24.4%) at Worker Reports and Lead Evidence.' 'Of the 301 pairs present at Source Reads, 106 also appear in Worker Reports (35.2%).' 'Worker Reports and Lead Evidence have identical labels, locating the observed handoff gap between source inspection and worker reporting.' 'Under None, source reads enter the lead’s evidence, so there is no drop between those two stages.' Matched cohorts (sec. 4.4; 'Same and Split cohorts are defined by Required’s observed evidence distribution, with None evaluated on the identical model, run, task, and conflict instances'): Source Reads Same, Required 38/111 (34.2%) vs None 25/111 (22.5%); Source Reads Split, 19/190 (10.0%) vs 36/190 (18.9%); 'Conditioning on Lead Evidence gives the same direction: 72.2% versus 33.3% for Same, and 17.1% versus 28.6% for Split.' Denominators of the Lead Evidence cohorts are not printed; Table 1's pooled Required Lead Evidence Same 16.4% and Split 8.0% of 438 give 72 and 35, hence 52/72 vs 24/72 and 6/35 vs 10/35 (inference). 'Shared-draft reads and arithmetic reconstruction can change a pair from Split at Source Reads to Same at Lead Evidence.' Worker omission by provenance (sec. 5): workers omit 'one or both claims in 73.2% of split-evidence cases compared with 50.5% when a single worker reads both'; of 190 Split and 111 Same pairs at Source Reads this is 139 and 56 omitted, 51 and 55 kept, summing to the 106 surviving pairs (inference). Delegation behaviour (sec. 4.2): under Optional 'Haiku creates workers in all 22 executions, whereas GPT-5.6 does so in 9/22 and GPT-6 in 10/22'; 'both GPT models’ Worker Reports achieve Pair Recall of only 0.7% (1/146) under Optional, compared with 24.0% under Required for GPT-5.6 and 18.5% for GPT-6'; Haiku's workers 37.0% under Optional and 30.8% under Required.
load_bearing_assumption: That both planted numbers appearing in the captured text of a stage is the same thing as the evidence being available there for a joint conclusion, and that a number missing from a worker's outgoing message is memory loss: 'A conflict earns pair credit when both endpoints are present, regardless of unrelated evidence' (sec. 3.4); 'Source evidence is counted from returned content, including search excerpts' (sec. 3.3). A number inside a tool dump the worker never attended to counts as read; a number absent from a summary that was asked for red flags, where the figure 'appear[s] unproblematic in isolation' (sec. 5), counts as a lost claim although leaving it out is what a faithful summary of one partition does; nothing in the text shows what the lead asked the worker for or what the worker wrote beyond the anchor match. If omission tracks what the brief asked for rather than what the worker could hold, the loss is a brief-design effect and 'memory inconsistency' is the wrong noun. Second, that None vs Required at matched dollars isolates delegation: the paper lists the bundle itself, 'Required combines mandatory delegation, partitioned source assignments, and restricted lead access, while model families use different SDKs' (Limitations), so the Split cohort (190 of 438 Required observations, Table 1 and sec. 4.4) is created by the partition, not by the summary; and because the planted edit sits in 'designated directories' (sec. 3.1), whether a partition boundary falls between $A_i$ and $B_i$ is set by the partitioning the lead chose, which the text does not report.
weakest_component: The sentence that locates the loss, 'the largest drop in evidence preservation at the worker-to-lead handoff' (sec. 1), read as a property of the return summary. The 44.3 pp fall from 301 to 107 of 438 (sec. 4.3) pools two different events. In 190 of the 301 retrieved pairs no single worker ever read both numbers (Split at Source Reads, 43.4% of 438, Table 1), so the worker that dropped a figure had no conflict to see, and the 73.2% omission rate there (sec. 5) measures the partition; in 111 pairs one worker held both and still dropped one or both in 50.5%, which is 56 of 438 or 12.8 pp (inference from sec. 5 and Table 1) and is the only part where a writer lost something it had. Against that, the single agent under None held both numbers in its own context in 220 of 438 (50.2%) and the judge passed 71 (16.2%): 149 pairs, 34.0 pp, lost inside one context with no handoff at all (inference from Table 1 pooled rows; the paper's matched version is Lead Evidence Same 72.2% vs 33.3%, sec. 4.4). The largest bucket of disappearing conflicts in Table 1 is the agent's own synthesis, and the summary-specific loss is the smallest of the three. Then: (1) no uncertainty estimates anywhere; the headline 16.2% vs 13.2% is about 71 vs 58 of 438 observations from 73 conflicts in 11 tasks run twice, 'with repeated conflicts clustered within tasks' (sec. 4.1), and the authors ask for 'uncertainty estimates accounting for shared tasks' (Limitations); (2) the matched cohorts condition on the treated arm's outcome, and None also scores higher on the Same cohorts (22.5% vs 18.9%; 33.3% vs 28.6%, sec. 4.4), so Same cases are easier for everyone; 'The matched groups also reflect agents’ observed retrieval and reporting choices' (Limitations); (3) the judge (claude-sonnet-5) is checked only this far: 'Manual inspection identified three saved Judge Pass labels that credited neighboring comparisons rather than the planted conflict' (Limitations), denominator not given, and the matcher is unvalidated; (4) 'Budgets were calibrated from observed spending, and GPT-5.6 Required checkpoints were selected retrospectively' (Limitations), in the cell with the lowest Judge Pass (10.3%, Table 1); (5) the two GPT models under Optional create workers in 9/22 and 10/22 executions and their workers supply a pair in 1/146 (sec. 4.2), so for GPT 'Optional' is a single agent with a budgeted second pass, and 'permitting overlapping source access and lead source inspection (Optional) consistently outperforms both single-agent and strictly partitioned execution' (sec. 5) rests on Haiku for anything delegation does; (6) harnesses differ by family (Codex SDK vs Claude Code SDK), so 'Required' is three implementations; (7) workers per execution, the lead's brief, worker-report length in tokens and the prompts are not in the text.
regime: Models: GPT-5.6 Luna and GPT-6 Luna through the Codex SDK, Claude Haiku 5.5 through the Claude Code SDK (sec. 4.1); lead and workers in one execution are the same model (the text reports one model per cell and never states a heterogeneous pairing; inference). Judge: claude-sonnet-5 (sec. 3.4). Tasks: 11 Harvey LAB due-diligence document-review tasks with a red-flags report as deliverable, 73 planted numerical conflicts, 5 to 7 per task (sec. 3.1). Policies: None, Optional, Required; up to ten concurrent workers plus further instances across continuation phases (sec. 3.2). Runs: 2 per model per policy, 198 executions, 1,314 conflict observations, 146 per model/policy, 438 per pooled policy (sec. 4.1). Budget: $59.60 per task per round, mean spend 0.95 to 1.02 of the allowance, compaction and paid interruptions counted, judging excluded (sec. 4.1; Table 1). Bands (Table 1): Source Reads Pair Recall 21.2% (Haiku None) to 78.8% (GPT-5.6 Required); Worker Reports Pair Recall 0.7% (GPT models, Optional) to 37.0% (Haiku Optional); Judge Pass 10.3% (GPT-5.6 Required) to 30.1% (Haiku Optional). Horizon in tokens, steps, tool calls or wall time: unknown (not in text). Workers per execution, brief and report lengths: unknown (not in text). Confidence intervals: none. Code, benchmark and profiler release: unknown (not in text). arXiv v2, 18 Nov 2026 (v1 17 Nov 2026 per the seed record); venue not stated; the v2 text carries an unremoved author comment in sec. 1 ('NOT SURE the definition is widely used. See my comment').
information_asymmetry: A conflict can vanish in three places, each a different asymmetry, and the paper measures them unequally. (1) Worker retrieval under partition. The lead sets the partition; the planted edit sits in 'designated directories' (sec. 3.1); whether $A_i$ and $B_i$ land in one worker's assignment is decided before any worker reads. Measured directly, from tool outputs (Source Reads). Pooled Required, 438 observations: both numbers read by someone in 301 (68.7%), by one worker in 111 (Same, 25.3%), only across workers in 190 (Split, 43.4%) (Table 1; cohort sizes in sec. 4.4). In those 190 the conflict exists only in the union of two contexts; no agent at that stage can see it, and the lead, which 'coordinates and synthesizes their findings without reading source documents' (sec. 3.2), does not know which worker read what. Information present in the system is absent from every single context. (2) The return summary. The worker holds its tool outputs; the lead receives only 'outgoing worker messages and completion reports, including peer-directed messages' (sec. 3.3). Measured directly, as the anchor match on sent messages, and receipts equal sends: 'Worker Reports and Lead Evidence have identical labels, locating the observed handoff gap between source inspection and worker reporting' (sec. 4.3). 'Of the 301 pairs present at Source Reads, 106 also appear in Worker Reports (35.2%)' (sec. 4.3); by provenance, workers omit 'one or both claims in 73.2% of split-evidence cases compared with 50.5% when a single worker reads both' (sec. 5), so 51 of 190 and 55 of 111 survive (inference; 51 + 55 = 106). The 56 Same losses (12.8% of 438, inference) are the only cases where a writer dropped something it held; the 139 Split losses are partition losses in a summary's clothing, because the worker that omitted a figure had no second figure to compare it with. Not measured: what the brief asked for, the report's length, whether the worker flagged anything itself, and when the figure was dropped ('The profiler measures cumulative evidence presence; tracing when both claims become jointly available would extend this analysis', Limitations); the mechanism offered, 'workers summarizing isolated partitions lack the cross-document context needed to recognize figures that appear unproblematic in isolation as conflicting across documents' (sec. 5), is inferred from the Same/Split rates, not read from any worker trace. (3) The lead's synthesis. The lead holds the reports; the judge sees the final report. Measured directly as Judge Pass by provenance cohort: with both numbers at the lead, Required passes 72.2% when one contributor supplied both and 17.1% when two did, None 33.3% and 28.6% on the same instances (sec. 4.4; denominators 72 and 35 by inference from Table 1). Not measured: anything inside the lead; 'conflict resolution depends heavily on provenance' (sec. 5) is the cohort difference restated. The number the paper does not foreground: under None the agent held both numbers in one context in 220 of 438 and the judge passed 71, so 149 conflicts (34.0 pp) vanish inside a single context (inference from Table 1 pooled rows), against 56 in the summary and 139 in the partition under Required; and Judge Pass divided by Lead Evidence Pair Recall is 16.2/50.2 = 0.32 under None and 13.2/24.4 = 0.54 under Required (inference), so a pair that survives a summary is flagged more often than a pair sitting in raw context, in the same direction as Lead Same 72.2% vs 33.3%. Inference: the summary is a filter that raises salience when it keeps the claim and erases the conflict when it does not; the paper measures the keep rate and not the salience effect as such. Standing asymmetries: forward vs hindsight, the profiler knows $G_i$ and the worker does not, and the worker is never told what to preserve ('Reporting interventions could then test whether preserving paired claims improves detection', Limitations); distribution vs retrieval, confounded by design ('Supplying identical evidence while varying which agents receive it would help separate the effect of distribution from retrieval difficulty', Limitations); training vs inference, none (nothing is trained). The missing ruler is per-return: given a fixed worker context that contains both numbers, the probability that the return carries both, as a function of brief wording, report length and model, with the lead's detection measured on injected reports carrying both, one, or both plus a flag; the 111 Same observations here are the natural seed set. The sibling card 2611.16526 (W46) measured the downward brief and inferred the upward loss; this paper measures the upward loss and never looks at the brief.
occupies: Published: a benchmark of 73 planted numerical conflicts over 11 Harvey LAB document-review tasks and an evidence-flow profiler with four stages (Source Reads, Worker Reports, Lead Evidence, Final Report) and a FEVER-style Pair Recall; with GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 under a common $59.60 per-task allowance, mandatory delegation raises retrieval of both claims from 50.2% to 68.7% and lowers judged detection from 16.2% to 13.2% of 438 pooled observations, Optional reaches 24.2% (Table 1); the loss is located between source inspection and worker reporting (301 to 107 of 438; 35.2% of retrieved pairs survive; sec. 4.3); on matched cases Required beats None when one worker read both claims (34.2% vs 22.5% of 111) and loses when they were split (10.0% vs 18.9% of 190), with the same direction at the lead (72.2% vs 33.3%; 17.1% vs 28.6%; sec. 4.4); and the design claim that 'permitting overlapping source access and lead source inspection (Optional) consistently outperforms both single-agent and strictly partitioned execution' (sec. 5). Stated as open by the paper itself: identical evidence with varied distribution, reporting interventions, the timing of joint availability, non-numerical conflicts and other domains, uncertainty estimates, human validation of the judge and the matcher.

theme_fit.why: the worker-to-lead return summary is the lane's object, measured as a keep rate for two specified claims (106 of 301 retrieved pairs, 35.2%, sec. 4.3) and costed in detection (13.2% vs 16.2% of 438, Table 1); the fetched compaction neighbour 2610.31778 (cited here as 'compaction can silently remove task constraints', sec. 2.1; its abstract: the first compaction summary drops about one third of ProgramBench's anticheating rules) is the self-to-self version of the same loss; what the lane still lacks is the per-return ruler at fixed worker context, which the Limitations name and do not run

a stage-wise attribution of one outcome to who moved (worker retrieval, worker report, lead synthesis) on a Harvey LAB benchmark, with the attribution's weaknesses in view: cohorts conditioned on the treated arm's outcome, 438 clustered observations from 11 tasks and two runs with no intervals, a judge checked by hand on an unstated denominator, retrospective checkpoints for one cell, three harness implementations

spending is the matching variable ($59.60 per task, 0.95 to 1.02 of allowance, compaction and paid interruptions counted, sec. 4.1) but nothing is reported in tokens, calls or time, so the cost side of delegation is a budget cap, not a measurement

limitations_as_complaints: My forced-delegation arm changes three things at once and my models run on different harnesses, so when a summary loses a claim I cannot say whether the partition, the lead's blindness to sources or the handoff did it, and my matched cohorts are sorted by what the treated arm happened to do: 'Required combines mandatory delegation, partitioned source assignments, and restricted lead access, while model families use different SDKs. The matched groups also reflect agents’ observed retrieval and reporting choices. Supplying identical evidence while varying which agents receive it would help separate the effect of distribution from retrieval difficulty' (Limitations).

I located the loss at the worker report but I never changed the report: no instruction to keep paired figures, no injected report carrying both claims, and my profiler only knows whether a number ever appeared, not when the two became jointly visible: 'The profiler measures cumulative evidence presence; tracing when both claims become jointly available would extend this analysis' (Limitations); 'Reporting interventions could then test whether preserving paired claims improves detection' (Limitations).

My headline is about 71 versus 58 detections out of 438 observations (16.2% vs 13.2%, Table 1) drawn from 73 conflicts in 11 tasks run twice, with no interval, my judge is checked by hand only far enough to find three false passes, and one cell's budget and checkpoints were set after the fact: 'Our evidence comes from 11 Harvey LAB tasks with planted numerical conflicts and two runs per model. Broader document domains, non-numerical conflicts, and more repetitions would test how widely the observed patterns hold, with uncertainty estimates accounting for shared tasks' (Limitations); 'Manual inspection identified three saved Judge Pass labels that credited neighboring comparisons rather than the planted conflict; broader human review could refine endpoint matching and semantic grading' (Limitations); 'Budgets were calibrated from observed spending, and GPT-5.6 Required checkpoints were selected retrospectively; future evaluations should fix budgets and checkpoint rules in advance' (Limitations).
